evidenceAudit.scope: Adults and children with diabetes on insulin or sulfonylureas in India who develop low blood glucose: recognition, treatment at home and in hospital, and prevention. Built on the ICMR Type 1 Diabetes workflow (July 2022) with the American Diabetes Association (ADA) 2025 Standards of Care for hypoglycaemia levels, the 15-gram rule and medicine review. Neonatal hypoglycaemia is a separate topic.
findings: Threshold below 70 mg/dL, severe definition, symptoms, oral glucose, glucagon 1 mg, 25% dextrose 1–2 mL/kg, monitoring for prevention and sick-day rules checked against the ICMR Type 1 Diabetes STW (July 2022).

Level 1–3 definitions, 15 g fast carbohydrate with recheck at 15 minutes, glucagon for insulin users and de-intensifying insulin or sulfonylureas taken from a summary of ADA Standards of Care 2025 section 6.
The ICMR Type 2 Diabetes STW (July 2022) was opened and contains no hypoglycaemia guidance.
Thiamine dose from the ICMR Alcohol Use Disorders STW.
unverifiedSections: Glucagon dose for small children is not varied by weight in the ICMR STW; check the product label.
The ADA content was read from a published summary, not the full Standards of Care text.
Prolonged sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia may need hours of dextrose infusion; infusion rate not given in the opened sources.
Drug cautions and contraindications without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.
US labels (DailyMed) were used where Indian sources give no dose; confirm against the Indian product label (CDSCO) and hospital formulary.

pathophysiology.summary: Hypoglycaemia is the commonest acute complication of diabetes treatment, caused by insulin or sulfonylureas when food, exercise and medicine are mismatched. The brain depends on glucose, so falling levels first trigger adrenergic warning symptoms (sweating, tremor, hunger) and then neuroglycopenia (confusion, drowsiness, seizures, coma). The ICMR workflow treats glucose below 70 mg/dL; severe hypoglycaemia means the person cannot treat themselves, has seizures or is unconscious. Every episode needs a cause and a medicine review (ADA).
keyMechanisms: Excess insulin or sulfonylurea effect suppresses liver glucose output and drives uptake into muscle.
Falling glucose triggers adrenaline release: sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger.
Neuroglycopenia causes confusion, behaviour change, seizures and coma.
Repeated episodes blunt warning symptoms, raising the risk of severe events.

symptoms: Sweating, hunger, tremor, irritability, weakness (ICMR STW)
Drowsiness, seizures or unconsciousness in late stages (ICMR STW)
Night sweats, nightmares or morning headache (nocturnal hypoglycaemia)
physicalSigns: Focal deficit that resolves with glucose
redFlags: Coma, seizures or unable to treat self: severe (ICMR STW)
Recurrent episodes or any severe episode: review medicines (ADA)
Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia: may recur for hours — admit
Hypoglycaemia in a heavy drinker or malnourished patient: give thiamine with glucose
precipitants: Missed or delayed meal; vomiting (ICMR sick-day rules)
Insulin or sulfonylurea dose too high (ADA)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Deficit persists after glucose is normal.
Breath alcohol; glucose may also be low — always check.
Glucose normal; symptoms do not respond to carbohydrate.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Mild or moderate: glucose below 70 mg/dL with or without symptoms. Severe: coma, seizures or unable to treat oneself.
Level 1: below 70 mg/dL. Level 2: below 54 mg/dL. Level 3: severe event needing assistance.
Recheck glucose 15 minutes after treatment and repeat if still low.
De-intensify insulin or sulfonylureas after recurrent moderate or any severe hypoglycaemia.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Below 70 mg/dL; below 54 mg/dL is level 2
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms and grades hypoglycaemia (ICMR STW; ADA).

clinicalManagement.title: Conscious and able to swallow
actions: Give fast-acting sugar: about 15 g (ADA), for example 3 teaspoons of glucose powder or sugar (ICMR STW).
Recheck in 15 minutes; repeat if still low (ADA).
Once above 70 mg/dL, give a snack or the next meal.

clinicalManagement.title: Severe (cannot swallow, seizure, unconscious)
actions: Caregiver gives glucagon 1 mg subcutaneous or intramuscular (ICMR STW).
In hospital: 25% dextrose 1–2 mL/kg IV (ICMR STW).
Place in recovery position; nothing by mouth until awake.

clinicalManagement.title: Admit or observe
actions: Admit sulfonylurea-related or recurrent hypoglycaemia for monitoring.
Give thiamine with glucose in heavy drinkers or the malnourished (ICMR AUD STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Prevent recurrence
actions: Find the mismatch between food, exercise and insulin (ICMR STW).
De-intensify insulin or sulfonylureas after recurrent or severe episodes (ADA).
Prescribe glucagon for insulin users and other high-risk patients (ADA).
Sick days: check glucose often, small meals 4–5 times a day, fluids (ICMR STW).

regimens.dose: 15 g (ADA); about 3 teaspoons of glucose powder or sugar (ICMR STW)
regimens.frequency: Repeat if glucose still below 70 mg/dL at 15 minutes
regimens.duration: Until glucose 70 mg/dL or more, then snack
adjustments: Paediatric: Children: same approach; smaller children may need less — seek paediatric advice.
Penicillin allergy: Not an antibiotic; penicillin allergy does not change this medicine.
CKD: No change; recheck more often (longer drug action).

medicationPlan.note: Oral glucose, glucagon and 25% dextrose doses are from the ICMR Type 1 Diabetes STW; the 15 g rule and recheck at 15 minutes from ADA 2025. Sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia can last many hours: admit and observe. Thiamine from the ICMR Alcohol Use Disorders STW. Not clinically reviewed.

keyPoints: 15 g fast sugar; recheck at 15 minutes.
Unconscious: 25% dextrose 1–2 mL/kg IV or glucagon 1 mg.
Review insulin and sulfonylurea doses after every severe episode.
pitfalls: Sending home a sulfonylurea overdose after one normal reading.
Oral sugar to a drowsy patient.
Not checking glucose in every confused or fitting patient.
